newsitem.title: UK: European air fares to rise after Q4 dip - Amex.
newsitem.headline: European air fares to rise after Q4 dip - Amex.

text.p: Air fares in western Europe are set to rise again in the early part of this year after a pause in average prices in late 1996, according to travel market analysts at American Express Co (Amex).
The latest edition of the company's European Airfare Index, covering the fourth quarter of 1996 and published on Tuesday, predicts that fares should soon track fuel prices and the dollar higher.

"This present stability is really just the calm before the storm," said Kyle Davis, head of the company's airfares management unit. However, Amex predicted that European market deregulation would remain a source of downward price pressure.

Davis said the impact of recent jet fuel price rises and the stronger dollar "were yet to be reflected in the index". This meant these technical factors were soon likely to add to upward price pressure which is normal in the busy northern hemisphere spring market, and force fares higher.
Although the Amex research is primarily aimed at the firm's business travel clients it also commented on the outlook for economy prices, including discounts, and excursion fares.

It noted that in the last quarter of 1996 first class fares in Europe rose by an average of two percent year-on-year, business class prices climbed by three percent, and full and discount economy fares rose one percent.
"The strong dollar is likely to affect fares in two ways," Davis said, anticipating rises in the early part of this year.

"Firstly, as jet fuel is traded in dollars, the price increases will be further compounded for European carriers. Secondly, fares from western Europe to the United States are bound to increase in order to close the growing gap between U.S. and European originating fares," he added.
Amex research shows that fares have risen generally at a greater rate than typical inflation over the past two years with quarterly increments often in the range of 1.0 to 1.5 percent.
Domestic excursion tickets are the only category of fares to show significant year-on-year falls in countries such as Italy, Germany and Sweden where competition has picked up recently.
This trend is fuelled by market preparations for the third and final package of European Union airline deregulation on April 1.
Amex predicted that the next likely effect of this pressure would be that some domestic business fares would also start to fall, as happened in Germany in the latter part of last year.
"Airline liberalisation is likely to start driving business type fares down in other domestic markets during 1997," it said.
